query: line following robot boundary tracking seed point image border lane line enters from side edge
content:
**In vision-based line-following robots or boundary-tracking systems (e.g., for autonomous navigation), seed points initiate algorithms like region-growing segmentation, flood fill, or contour/boundary tracing (such as Moore-neighbor tracing) to follow lane lines or road boundaries in camera images.**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_tracing)[[2]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3311951)

Standard practice places seed points in the lower-central portion of the image (near the bottom border), where the forward-facing camera reliably sees the path or lane ahead on the ground plane. This assumes a typical perspective where the navigable surface occupies the bottom of the frame.[[2]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3311951)[[3]](https://rvsn.csail.mit.edu/Pubs/phd_ashuang_2010feb_laneestimation.pdf)

### Handling Lane Lines Entering from Side Edges
When a lane line or boundary "enters from the side edge" (i.e., intersects the left or right border of the image rather than originating near the bottom), it typically signals:
- The robot/vehicle is laterally offset from the line.
- A sharp curve or turn where the line sweeps across the frame.
- Partial occlusion, loss of the bottom view, or the line running along the side of the field of view.

This breaks assumptions in bottom-seeded methods, as the line pixels may not appear in the expected lower ROI.[[4]](https://medium.com/data-science/lane-detection-with-deep-learning-part-1-9e096f3320b7)

**Techniques to address this** include:

1. **Adaptive or Border-Based Seed Point Selection** — Instead of (or in addition to) bottom seeds, scan the left and right image borders for qualifying pixels (e.g., dark/black pixels on a light background for a black line, or edge-detected transitions). Use the lowest or most central such point as a seed for region growing or boundary tracing. Some systems divide the image into horizontal slices and analyze bottom-up or use Otsu thresholding per slice to locate road/lane candidates dynamically.[[2]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3311951)[[2]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3311951)

2. **Boundary/Contour Tracing from Border Intersections** — Apply binarization (thresholding) to isolate the line, then use algorithms like Moore-neighbor tracing. Start tracing from a detected boundary pixel on the side edge and follow neighbors (clockwise or counterclockwise) around the contour. This naturally handles lines that clip the frame sides.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_tracing)[[5]](https://www.scribd.com/document/952690402/Computer-Vision-Unit-4-Boundary-Tracking-Procedures)

3. **Sliding Window or Histogram-Based Detection with Side Handling** — In lane detection pipelines (common for robots and vehicles), use vertical histograms or sliding windows on a bird’s-eye or warped view. When a window touches the side border, stop extending it upward to avoid false vertical extrapolation; instead, treat the side intersection as the line’s entry point. Peak detection on left/right halves of the image can initialize separate left/right lane searches.[[4]](https://medium.com/data-science/lane-detection-with-deep-learning-part-1-9e096f3320b7)[[6]](https://www.hackster.io/kemfic/curved-lane-detection-34f771)

4. **Hybrid Approaches (Edges + Region Growing + Geometry)** — Combine Canny/Sobel edge detection or Hough transform (to find lines intersecting borders) with region growing from multiple candidate seeds. Vanishing-point estimation or road-border rays can help define a bisector and place a seed point even when sides dominate. For sharp curves, spline fitting or dynamic seed propagation from prior frames maintains tracking.[[7]](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/17/9/2101)[[3]](https://rvsn.csail.mit.edu/Pubs/phd_ashuang_2010feb_laneestimation.pdf)

5. **Additional Robustness Measures**:
   - Use a region of interest (ROI) that adapts based on prior detections or includes side margins.
   - Temporal tracking (e.g., Kalman filter or previous-frame seeds) predicts line position and seeds the current frame.
   - Multi-seed or superpixel methods to sample across the image rather than relying on one bottom location.[[2]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3311951)

### Practical Implementation Notes (e.g., OpenCV-Style)
- Binarize → find contours or use `findContours` / custom Moore tracing starting from border pixels.
- For seeds: Scan columns at image edges (`image[0 to height, 0]` and `image[0 to height, width-1]`) for line-like pixels.
- Handle edge cases: If no valid seed on bottom or sides, fall back to full-image search, previous-frame prediction, or stop/slow the robot.
- Real-world analogy: Think of the image as a forward windshield view; the line normally runs “under the hood” (bottom), but on a hard left turn it may “enter through the driver’s side window” (left edge)—your algorithm must “look sideways” to pick it up.

These methods appear in road-detection literature for mobile robots and vehicles, where region-based approaches excel at unstructured surfaces without relying solely on painted lane markings.[[2]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3311951)[[7]](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/17/9/2101) Performance depends on lighting, camera calibration, and thresholding—test with varied offsets and curves. Authoritative sources emphasize starting seeds low in the frame but adapting for robustness.
